Putting greens for lots backing the Hunter's Creek fairways

A backyard putting green in Hunters Creek runs $14–$30 per square foot as of September 2026, reflecting the contouring, fringe turf and cups a green needs beyond a flat lawn. Hunter's Creek Golf Club, built in 1986 and once ranked among Golf Digest's top public courses, backs directly onto a number of the community's own lots, and homeowners asking about the best putting-green builder near Hunters Creek are usually the ones with a fairway view already.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

A fairway view changes the ARC drawing, not just the yard

A lot backing one of Hunter's Creek Golf Club's fairways carries the same buffer the HCCA applies to any pond- or lake-facing yard: a low picket fence set within 20 feet of the rear line, with hedges capped at 18 inches inside that zone. A green on that kind of lot has to fit inside the buffer rather than running its contour up to the fence, which usually means a smaller footprint than the flat rectangle a green would ideally want. The association still treats a putting surface as artificial turf for review purposes, so the same case-by-case, rear-yard-only application applies whether the finished product is a lawn or a contoured green with a collar and cups.

Why washed rock matters more under a putting surface

The same rule requiring washed rock under any Hunters Creek lawn applies to a putting green's base, and the consequences of skipping it show up faster here than almost anywhere else on the property. Fines from unwashed fill binding into a crust don't just slow drainage the way they would under a lawn; they also create an uneven surface underneath the shaped tiers, which shows up as a dead spot or an unexpected bounce exactly where a ball should be rolling true. A green's fine tolerance for surface consistency makes a crusted, uneven base far more noticeable in daily use than the same problem would be under grass nobody's testing with a putter.

Why a green needs more grading attention on this soil

The flatwoods sands common across south Orange County drain slowly and sit close to a seasonally high water table, which matters more on a putting green than on a flat lawn because a green's whole purpose depends on a subgrade that holds its shape through a rainy Central Florida summer without a low spot forming under the nylon surface. Getting the base right here takes more attention to layered compaction and to the crown and contour built into the crushed rock itself, not just a deeper base the way a dog run gets. A green built on an undercompacted base in this soil is the build most likely to develop a dip inside its first year.

Cups: the hardware inside a green's design

Cups are cored directly through the finished base at whatever locations the break design calls for, then set and edged so they sit flush with the surrounding putting surface on a Hunters Creek green. The number and placement of cups is as much a product decision as the turf fiber itself, since each one interrupts the shaped surface and has to be positioned where the breaks actually make sense to putt toward. Adding cups after the surface is already down means recutting finished turf, which is why cup locations get fixed during the design phase rather than adjusted later.

Say you have a 450 sq ft green on a fairway-backing lot

Say you have a 450 sq ft putting and chipping green planned for a lot backing Hunter's Creek Golf Club's back nine, with the green's edge held 21 feet off the rear line to clear the HCCA's 20-foot buffer with a foot to spare. At the published $14–$30 per sq ft range, that green prices between $6,300 and $13,500 installed, typically $18–$25: about $8,100 to $11,250 for the full 450 sq ft, with contouring and a fringe collar pushing toward the top of that range rather than the bottom.

Seaming the putting surface and fringe as separate pieces

The short putting surface and the taller fringe turf around a Hunters Creek green get cut and seamed as two distinct pieces rather than one continuous roll, since they're different products at different pile heights doing different jobs. That seam is placed deliberately along the design's edge line so it reads as a mowing transition once grooming is finished, not as a visible patch where two products meet. Getting this seam line right the first time matters more on a green than on a lawn, since the edge is exactly where a chip shot lands and a rough transition is the most visible spot on the entire surface.

Drip lines and a shaded green under mature oaks

The same drip-line rule that keeps turf away from a live oak's roots applies to a putting green, and a shaded spot under mature canopy that looks appealing for a Hunters Creek green during the hottest months still requires a certified arborist's sign-off before any shaping or excavation happens nearby. Excavating four to six inches for a green's base is deeper than a lawn conversion, which makes root damage a bigger risk under canopy than it would be for grass alone. Choosing a different, sunnier spot for the green and keeping the shaded area as fringe or lawn instead is often the simpler path.

Golf Club history, and why a home green still isn't the same game

Hunter's Creek Golf Club opened in 1986 and was named one of Golf Digest's Top 75 Public Courses in 1990, anchoring the community's identity since its earliest villages went in. A backyard green built off that reputation is still a different product: home greens use a synthetic surface built for a consistent roll at a modest size, not the maintained natural turf a public course runs, and a good installer sets stimp speed and slope through the base contour rather than through mowing height. The association's application doesn't distinguish a green from any other artificial turf request, so the same substrate and drainage requirements apply regardless of how elaborate the contouring gets.

Topping off infill on a putting surface

A Hunters Creek green's infill thins gradually with every rinse, rainstorm, and round played on it, and because the putting surface is groomed to a tighter tolerance than a lawn, that gradual loss shows up in how a ball rolls before it's ever visible to the eye. Adding a light layer back in every year or two, rather than waiting for a visibly bare patch to appear, keeps the roll behaving the way it did on day one instead of drifting toward faster or bouncier as the months add up. Checking depth on a set schedule beats waiting for a complaint about a mis-hit putt to prompt the work.

Questions people ask

Does living on a golf-course lot in Hunters Creek make ARC approval easier for a green?

No. The Architectural Review Committee treats a putting green the same as any other back-yard turf request, so the substrate depth, drainage direction and 20-foot fence buffer all still apply regardless of the fairway view.

Can a green extend past the HCCA's fence line toward the fairway?

No, the green has to stay on the homeowner's side of the association's fence buffer, which sits within 20 feet of the rear property line on a fairway lot; the course itself is never part of the layout.
